analysis.one_liner: Orders OSHA to set binding limits on workplace exposure to diacetyl, the butter-flavoring chemical linked to a fatal lung disease.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 260-154 in September 2007, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Diacetyl is a chemical used in artificial butter flavoring. Workers who breathe it in factories making flavorings and microwave popcorn developed bronchiolitis obliterans, a serious and often irreversible lung disease. Despite a federal safety institute finding the danger and labor groups petitioning for emergency rules, OSHA had issued no standard limiting exposure. This bill would have forced the Labor Department to issue a legally binding interim standard within 90 days—venting, respirators, air monitoring, medical checks for exposed workers—and a permanent exposure limit within two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in flavoring-manufacturing plants and microwave popcorn production and packaging facilities, who would gain mandatory ventilation and closed processes, airborne exposure testing, protective equipment, medical surveillance, and training instead of voluntary recommendations. Most would be low-wage production and mixing workers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an interim OSHA standard within 90 days covering all flavoring plants and all microwave popcorn production and packaging sites that use diacetyl, with the legal force of an OSHA standard until a final rule takes effect [S3] [S4] [S5].

Mandates engineering controls such as closed processes and exhaust ventilation, written exposure control plans, airborne exposure assessments, protective equipment and clothing, medical surveillance with prompt medical referral, and written hazard training [S3] [S4] [S5].

Requires a final standard within two years setting a short-term exposure limit and a permissible exposure limit no higher than the lowest feasible level, applying to every facility where diacetyl is processed or used [S4] [S5].
Directs NIOSH to study flavoring chemicals used as diacetyl substitutes and recommend exposure limits, so replacements would not repeat the same hazard [S4] [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Flavoring manufacturers and microwave popcorn producers would bear the cost of ventilation, closed processes, respirators, air monitoring, and medical surveillance programs. Those costs could be partly passed to consumers in slightly higher prices for flavored products.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have bypassed OSHA's normal rulemaking process by imposing an interim standard within 90 days with no notice-and-comment period, a fast track critics said was legally unusual and left no room to test whether the specific limits were workable across different plants [S5].

Compliance costs for ventilation, closed processes, and medical surveillance would fall on flavoring and popcorn companies, including smaller firms, and could be partially passed on to consumers [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes were severe: bronchiolitis obliterans is a debilitating, often permanent lung disease, and federal scientists had already linked it to diacetyl exposure and published recommended protections that employers were only following voluntarily [S5]. The main cost is compliance spending by a small set of food-flavoring and popcorn facilities. A fair objection is the 90-day rulemaking shortcut, but the underlying protections were drawn from an existing federal safety alert rather than invented from scratch.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 260-154, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote; it simply sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Education and Labor Committee reported the bill amended on July 18, 2007, and placed it on the Union Calendar [S7].
The House passed the bill on September 26, 2007, by a vote of 260-154 with 2 present (Roll no. 913): 213 of 231 Democrats and 47 of 201 Republicans voted yes [S7] [S8].
The Senate received the bill on September 27, 2007, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 400) on September 28 [S7] [S5].
No further Senate action is recorded; the bill never received a Senate vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S7] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Flavoring manufacturers and microwave popcorn producers avoided binding federal exposure limits, and OSHA faced no new legal deadline to regulate diacetyl; workers in those plants remained covered only by voluntary recommendations.

for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, joining a bipartisan majority [S8].

against.name: Senate leadership of the 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the calendar; it received no floor action, committee or otherwise, for the rest of the Congress [S7].

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split mainly by party: 213-8 among Democrats for the bill, but Republicans opposed it 146-47, producing the 260-154 final margin.

industries.note: The bill would have required closed processes, ventilation, respirators, air monitoring, and medical surveillance at every plant handling diacetyl—costs the industry was otherwise bearing only voluntarily under its own safety guidance [S5]. Its interest in avoiding binding limits ran against workers' interest in not developing irreversible lung disease.

Popcorn production and packaging facilities using diacetyl-containing flavors would have been directly covered by the interim standard, adding compliance costs; some producers had already reformulated to drop diacetyl, which the bill's final-standard trigger recognized [S4] [S5].
